description_ru: Аспирантка приходит к научному руководителю с провалившимся повторением эксперимента. Разговор о том, чем ценна неудача и как превратить её в главу диссертации.
text:
Lena: Dr Okafor, have you got a minute? I'd rather not wait until Thursday's meeting, because I suspect I'll lose my nerve.
Okafor: Come in, sit down. You look as though you've been awake since Tuesday. What's happened?
Lena: The replication failed. I ran the full protocol three times, with the larger sample, and the effect simply isn't there. Not weaker, not noisy. Absent.
Okafor: Ah. And how many times did you check the analysis before telling me?
Lena: Embarrassingly, about forty. I even had Marcus go through the code line by line. There's no bug.

Okafor: Good. That's the correct reaction, and I'm sorry to say it's also the beginning of a long afternoon. Sit.
Okafor: And your instinct is to blame yourself, I imagine, rather than the universe.
Lena: Naturally. The universe has a perfect record, and I have a pipette and a bad attitude.
Okafor: Then let me offer a different hypothesis, which is that the universe has simply declined to cooperate with a rather fashionable idea.

Lena: The thing is, the whole second chapter depends on it. If the original finding doesn't hold, I don't have a chapter. I might not have a thesis.
Okafor: Let's slow down. What you have is a clean, well-powered null result. In a sense, that's rarer than a positive one.
Lena: With respect, that sounds like something people say at funerals.
Okafor: It does, doesn't it? But I mean it. Do you know how many labs have quietly failed to reproduce that paper and said nothing?
Lena: I didn't realise there were any.

Okafor: Because nobody publishes them. Journals love a surprise, and a failure to find something is rarely a surprise. So the original result sits there, unchallenged, and a hundred students build on it like a house on sand.
Lena: So I'm the one who gets to discover the sand.
Okafor: Precisely. Which is uncomfortable, and also, if you handle it properly, a rather significant contribution.
Lena: Dr Okafor, I appreciate the optimism, but the committee wants a story. A coherent arc. I can hardly walk in and say, "Here are three years of nothing."
Okafor: Not nothing. Think about what you've actually done. You've tested a claim that shaped a subfield, with greater rigour than anyone before you. That is the job, Lena. We pretend it's about confirming things, but science is mostly the patient business of discovering where our confidence was misplaced.

Lena: It doesn't feel like that at two in the morning.
Okafor: No. It never does. May I tell you something I don't usually admit to students?
Lena: Please.
Okafor: In my second year, I spent eighteen months chasing a protein interaction that turned out to be an artefact of the buffer I was using. A contaminant. Eighteen months. I nearly left the field.
Lena: What stopped you?

Okafor: A rather blunt postdoc named Hartmann, who told me that the only people who never waste time are those who never try anything. Then he made me present the failure at group meeting, with slides.
Lena: That sounds mortifying.
Okafor: It was. It was also the most useful talk I've ever given, because a visiting professor in the audience recognised the same artefact in his own data and spent the following month rescuing a paper of his. Failures, it turns out, are communal property, if you're brave enough to share them.
Lena: All right. Suppose I accept that this is valuable. How do I make it a chapter?

Okafor: By changing the question. Instead of asking whether the effect exists, ask why the original appeared to. There must have been something in that first experiment, a quirk in the stimuli, a lucky subset, a flexible analysis, that produced the signal.
Lena: Which means going back through their methods. Politely, I assume.
Okafor: Exceedingly politely. Remember that the original authors weren't villains. They probably did exactly what everyone did at the time. The incentives rewarded it.
Lena: And if they get defensive?
Okafor: Then you'll have a perfect example of why we need open data. But I suspect you'll find them more generous than you expect. Most researchers would rather learn the truth in a friendly email than on a conference stage.

Lena: I could preregister the new analysis. Be transparent about every decision.
Okafor: Now you're thinking like a scientist rather than a candidate. I'd go further. Write to them before you publish. Offer them the data. Make it collaborative.
Lena: That's a risk, isn't it? What if they try to block it?
Okafor: Possibly, although I doubt it. Most editors respond well to a manuscript that is honest about its own limitations and generous about everybody else's.
Lena: I'd like to believe that.

Okafor: Believe it provisionally. That's what we do. A result that survives only because nobody was allowed to look at it isn't worth protecting. And I'll back you, if it comes to that. I have tenure for a reason.
Lena: I don't know what to say.
Okafor: Say that you'll go home, sleep for ten hours, and eat something that didn't come out of a vending machine. We'll rewrite the outline on Monday.
Lena: Thank you. Honestly. I came in here expecting to be consoled, and instead I've been given a plan.

Lena: What if the committee asks why I didn't see the problem earlier?
Okafor: Then you'll explain that nobody could have seen it earlier, because the evidence didn't exist until you produced it. That is the entire point of an experiment.
Okafor: Consolation is cheap, and it wears off by Wednesday. A plan lasts.
Lena: May I ask one more thing? Do you still think about those eighteen months?
Okafor: Every time I'm tempted to trust a result because I want it to be true. It's a better teacher than any of my successes. Now go home, Lena, before I start being sentimental.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение: repliˈcation, ˈincentives, comˈmunal (в американском варианте на -mu-). Слоги перед ударением редуцируйте до «ə».
Конечный «d» в good, planned, rewrite-ed словах должен оставаться звонким, а не превращаться в «т».
Для «th» (thesis, three, think) язык слегка высунут между зубами, звук глухой.
Связывайте слова: look_at_it, think_about звучат слитно.

questions.question: What went wrong with Lena's experiment?
questions.answer: The replication failed: the effect was absent even with a larger sample.

questions.question: Why does Dr Okafor call the null result valuable?
questions.answer: Because few journals publish failures, so the original claim stays unchallenged.

questions.question: What mistake did Dr Okafor make in his second year?
questions.answer: He chased a protein interaction that was an artefact of the buffer.

questions.question: What does he advise Lena to do?
questions.answer: Ask why the original appeared to work, and contact the original authors collaboratively.
